**How it works:** the trick is that the two compilers treat a backslash at the end of a line differently.
- In C++, a backslash at the end of a line joins it to the next line. So a `//\` comment also swallows the line after it.
- In Rust, `//\` is just an ordinary comment that ends at the end of its line.

**How the file is laid out:**
```
//\
/*
  ... C++ program ...
//\
*/
//\
fn main(){ ... Rust program on one line ... }
```
- **Rust** sees a line comment, then a `/* ... */` block comment around all the C++ code, then the `fn main` line, which it compiles.
- **C++** treats the first `//\` and the `/*` line as a single comment, so it compiles the C++ program normally. Each later `//\` swallows the line after it, which hides the closing `*/` and the whole Rust line.

Both versions add numbers stored as chunks of 9 decimal digits, so they don't overflow at large N.

The C++ code must never contain `/*` or `*/`. Rust allows nested block comments, so either one would break the Rust side.
